topic: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the mass of product collected is almost always less than the calculated amount. What does this shortfall show?
items.correct: The atoms all still exist, but they are not all in the product.
items.misconception: A few of the atoms are destroyed as the old bonds are broken apart.
items.why: Conservation of mass is learnt as a rule about sealed flasks, so when the balance reads short students look for missing matter instead of asking where the matter went. Ask where the atoms are, not whether they still exist. Name one of the three destinations the specification allows: still unreacted, left behind during separation, or built into a different product.
items.random_wrong: Mass is conserved only when a reaction is done in a sealed flask.

items.q: A product is made using a reaction that is reversible. Why does this keep the yield below the maximum theoretical amount?
items.correct: The reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is left over.
items.misconception: All of the product turns back into the reactants, and none is left.
items.why: The double arrow is read as 'it goes backwards' rather than as 'both directions happen at the same time', so students imagine the forward reaction being completely undone. Both reactions run together and settle at a balance point. There is always some product present, just less than the equation on its own predicts.
items.random_wrong: Atoms are used up by the backward reaction and cannot be got back.

items.q: Copper sulfate crystals are filtered from the reaction mixture, washed and dried before being weighed. Which reason for a low yield does this practical show?
items.correct: Some product stays on the filter paper and inside the glassware.
items.misconception: Filtering strips atoms out of the compound, so it now weighs less.
items.why: The word 'lost' is read as a loss from each particle rather than as a loss of whole particles from the sample being weighed. Separation removes some of the crystals, not part of each crystal. What is weighed is pure product; there is simply less of it.
items.random_wrong: Water driven off during drying shows mass is not conserved.

items.q: A student analyses the product mixture and finds an unexpected second compound in it. Which reason for the reduced yield does this point to?
items.correct: Some reactant reacted in a way different to the expected one.
items.misconception: The reaction is reversible, so some product has changed back again.
items.why: Reversibility is the first reason students learn and becomes a catch-all explanation for anything that is not the pure expected product. A reversible reaction leaves the original reactants behind, not a brand new compound. A new compound points to some reactant taking a different reaction pathway.
items.random_wrong: Filtering and washing took some atoms out of the product itself.

items.q: What does the percentage yield of a reaction tell you?
items.correct: The mass of product made, as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass.
items.misconception: The percentage of the product that has not turned back into reactants.
items.why: The double arrow is read as 'it goes backwards' rather than as 'both directions happen at the same time', so students imagine the forward reaction being completely undone. Both reactions run together and settle at a balance point. There is always some product present, just less than the equation on its own predicts.
items.random_wrong: The mass of product made, as a percentage of the mass of the reactants.

items.q: Which calculation gives the percentage yield of a product?
items.correct: (mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100
items.misconception: (maximum theoretical mass of product / mass of the product made) x 100
items.why: Students remember that two masses are divided but not which one is on top, and the theoretical mass is the larger number, which feels like a natural numerator. Check the answer: a yield above 100 % is impossible, so any answer over 100 % means the fraction was written upside down.
items.random_wrong: (mass of product actually made / total mass of all reactants) x 100

items.q: 6.0 g of magnesium is burned in air. The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 10.0 g. The student collects 8.5 g of magnesium oxide. What is the percentage yield?
items.why: The reactant mass is usually the first number in the question, and students who have not fixed the formula reach for the number they met first. Both masses in the fraction refer to the same product. If one of the numbers is a reactant, it does not belong in the fraction.

items.q: The maximum theoretical mass of a product is 60 g. A student separates and dries the product and obtains 54 g of it. What is the percentage yield?
items.why: Students remember that two masses are divided but not which one is on top, and the theoretical mass is the larger number, which feels like a natural numerator. Check the answer: a yield above 100 % is impossible, so any answer over 100 % means the fraction was written upside down.

items.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 10 g of calcium carbonate?
items.why: The relative formula masses are the most visible numbers in the working, so students report them, or combine them as a ratio without checking which way up it goes. Ask how many moles there are. Only when it is exactly one mole does the relative formula mass equal the mass in grams.

items.q: Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr: Fe2O3 = 160, Fe = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron that can be made from 20 g of iron(III) oxide?
items.why: The relative formula masses are the most visible numbers in the working, so students report them, or combine them as a ratio without checking which way up it goes. Ask how many moles there are. Only when it is exactly one mole does the relative formula mass equal the mass in grams.

items.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?
items.correct: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful product.
items.misconception: The amount of the predicted product that is collected in practice.
items.why: Yield and atom economy are taught together, both are percentages and both describe efficiency, so the two definitions blur into one. Yield is measured in the laboratory and changes with technique; atom economy comes from the equation and is the same every time the reaction is used.
items.random_wrong: The amount of reactant that has reacted once equilibrium has been set up.

items.q: A student weighs out the reactants, weighs the product she has made and divides one measured mass by the other to find the atom economy. Why is this wrong?
items.correct: The percentage atom economy is calculated using the balanced equation.
items.misconception: The mass lost when the product was separated must be subtracted.
items.why: Percentage yield uses masses from the balance, so students assume the other percentage in this topic must use them too. Atom economy is fixed by the equation. It is the same figure whether the reaction is done well or badly, and on any scale.
items.random_wrong: The atom economy changes when the reaction is scaled up to industry.

items.q: In the percentage atom economy calculation, what is the bottom line of the fraction?
items.correct: The sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants in the equation.
items.misconception: The relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation.
items.why: The formula is remembered as two relative formula masses divided, with no check on which one is the numerator. Put the desired product on top. Any answer above 100 % shows that the fraction was inverted.
items.random_wrong: The relative formula mass of the one reactant that the product comes from.

items.q: Hydrogen is made from methane: CH4 + H2O -> 3H2 + CO. Mr: CH4 = 16, H2O = 18, H2 = 2, CO = 28. What is the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen?
items.why: Students trace the atoms of interest back to one reactant and treat the other reactants as if they were not really starting materials. Every reactant had to be supplied and paid for, so every reactant counts in the bottom line, each multiplied by its balancing number.

items.q: Titanium is extracted by the reaction TiCl4 + 4Na -> Ti + 4NaCl. Mr: TiCl4 = 190, Na = 23, Ti = 48, NaCl = 58.5. What is the percentage atom economy for titanium?
items.why: The formula is remembered as two relative formula masses divided, with no check on which one is the numerator. Put the desired product on top. Any answer above 100 % shows that the fraction was inverted.

items.q: Two routes make the same product. Route 1: atom economy 42 %, percentage yield 95 %, fast, by-product is waste that must be disposed of. Route 2: atom economy 88 %, percentage yield 90 %, slightly slower, by-product is sold as a fertiliser. Which judgement is best supported by the data?
items.correct: Route 2, because much more of the reactant mass ends up as product.
items.misconception: Route 1, because its higher percentage yield means that less is wasted.
items.why: Yield and rate are the more familiar figures and the larger number looks better, so one figure is treated as the whole answer. Compare the figures separately: yield says how much of the possible product was captured, atom economy says how much of the raw material could ever have become product.
items.random_wrong: Route 1, because a faster rate always makes the process a cheaper one.

items.q: Give one reason why it is important for a company to use a reaction with a high atom economy.
items.correct: Less of the starting material is wasted, so raw materials cost less.
items.misconception: More of the product predicted by the equation is collected each time.
items.why: Yield and atom economy are taught together, both are percentages and both describe efficiency, so the two definitions blur into one. Yield is measured in the laboratory and changes with technique; atom economy comes from the equation and is the same every time the reaction is used.
items.random_wrong: The reaction runs faster, so more product is made in the same time.

items.q: Does a yield below 100 % show that mass was not conserved?
items.correct: No. Mass is conserved in every chemical reaction, sealed or open. A low yield describes where the product ended up, not how much matter exists.
items.misconception: Mass is only conserved if the reaction is carried out in a sealed container, so an open reaction can genuinely lose mass.
items.why: Students meet conservation of mass through demonstrations in stoppered flasks and meet apparent mass changes in open crucibles, so they attach the law to the apparatus rather than to the atoms. In an open vessel the atoms leave the vessel; they are not destroyed. Weighing everything, including any gas, always gives the same total.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does percentage yield compare?
items.correct: The mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass of that product, as a percentage.
items.misconception: Percentage yield compares the mass of product with the mass of reactants that were used, or reports the percentage that was lost.
items.why: It sounds like an efficiency, and the reactant mass is the first number the student weighed out, so it feels like the natural thing to divide by. The comparison is product against predicted product, and it is the amount obtained that goes on top, not the amount missing.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student divides 54 by 60 and writes 0.9. What has been missed?
items.correct: The ratio must be multiplied by 100 to turn it into a percentage, giving 90.0 %.
items.misconception: The decimal answer from the division is the percentage yield.
items.why: The division feels like the chemistry, so the x 100 at the end of the formula is treated as decoration and dropped. A percentage is a number per hundred. If the answer comes out as a decimal below 1, the x 100 has been forgotten.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide from 10 g of calcium carbonate?
items.correct: 10 g of CaCO3 is 0.1 mol, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the theoretical mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.
items.misconception: Mass is conserved, so 10 g of calcium carbonate must give 10 g of calcium oxide.
items.why: Conservation of mass is over-applied: the total mass of all the products is 10 g, but the carbon dioxide escapes and carries part of it away. Mass is conserved across all the products together, not for one product on its own. Work in moles and use the relative formula mass of the product asked for.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Why is 7 g of iron from 20 g of iron(III) oxide wrong?
items.correct: 0.125 mol of Fe2O3 gives 0.25 mol of Fe because of the 2 in front of Fe, so the mass is 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.
items.misconception: Only one atom of the desired element counts, so the product mass is the reactant mass times that element's Ar over the reactant's Mr, ignoring balancing numbers and any other atoms in the product.
items.why: Students convert mass to moles confidently and then jump straight to the relative formula mass of the product, skipping the mole ratio step entirely. Always read the balancing numbers as a mole ratio. Write the ratio down, here 1 : 2, before multiplying by the relative formula mass.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the atom economy always 100 % because no atoms are lost?
items.correct: No. All the atoms are still present, but those in the by-products are not in the useful product, so the atom economy is below 100 % whenever the equation shows more than one product.
items.misconception: Since no atoms are gained or lost, all of the starting material ends up as useful product.
items.why: Conservation of mass is confused with usefulness: students count all the atoms as 'used' whichever compound they end up in. Only one product is wanted. The atom economy is 100 % only when the equation shows a single product.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a high atom economy guarantee a high percentage yield?
items.correct: No. They are independent. A reaction with a single product has an atom economy of 100 % but may still be reversible or lose product on separation, giving a low yield.
items.misconception: A high atom economy means most of the product will be collected, so the yield must be high as well.
items.why: Both are percentages describing efficiency, so students expect them to rise and fall together. Atom economy comes from the equation, yield from the laboratory. Either one can be high while the other is low.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.3.3 Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
